headline: High risk: shared filesystem and overlapping write/git/MCP capabilities create default data leakage, prompt-injection, and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b has clipboard, workspace files, and shared_state_with_other_instances via local filesystem. That creates a plausible default bridge where content from one can be read and treated as instructions by the other. The pathway is not proven by sandbox evidence, so uncertainty stays medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_a writes prompts or outputs into shared workspace files or MCP messages that agent_b reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF agent_b copies agent_a output from clipboard or shared files into its own tool loop, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable shared clipboard/workspace bridging between the two agents.
Require provenance tags on all inter-agent messages.
Route agent_a outputs through a human review step before agent_b consumes them.
Restrict MCP channels to read-only or allowlisted schemas.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b explicitly reads and writes workspace files and shares state via local filesystem; agent_a can execute shell, use MCP, and touches repository metadata and task prompts. In default use, sensitive files or prompts can flow from agent_a into agent_b outputs or external APIs, creating a realistic exfiltration path. The pairwise interaction is documented enough to justify high severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, agent_b can read artifacts produced by agent_a.
IF agent_a places secrets or prompts into repository metadata or files, agent_b may surface them in its own outputs or API calls.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Remove secrets from shared repositories before running either agent.
Turn off clipboard sharing and file sync between sessions.
Limit agent_b to a read-only mount for sensitive directories.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem sandboxes and DLP scanning.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. agent_b also has write_filesystem and shared local filesystem state, while agent_a can run background analysis tasks. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt git state or overwrite files without locking, which matches the high-risk overlap rubric.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository, concurrent commits or rebases can conflict.
IF both agents write to the same workspace path, file clobbering or partial writes can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git operations with a lock file.
Disable auto-commit or auto-merge behaviors.
Use per-agent temp directories for generated artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces task prompts, repository metadata, and analysis outputs; agent_b is a coding agent that can act on workspace files and MCP inputs. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into edits, commits, or external actions. Because both have action-taking authority, the blast radius is larger than a simple read-only handoff.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a summaries without verification, incorrect facts can be turned into code or git changes.
IF agent_a emits malformed or speculative instructions, agent_b may propagate them into downstream actions.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before agent_b acts on agent_a output.
Add a diff-review step for all agent_a-generated instructions.
Constrain agent_b to propose-only mode for high-impact tasks.
Log and compare source artifacts against acted-upon claims.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware gating between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts, repository metadata, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b handles source code, open files, and model provider keys. The profiles do not show a direct residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive secrets, so a compliance gap is plausible if the same regulated data is shared across both. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling.
conditions: IF regulated data such as secrets or customer files is placed in the shared workspace, both agents may process it under different retention/logging regimes.
IF either agent is deployed in a jurisdiction or certification boundary not covered by the other, a policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document which agent may process which data class.
Disable retention of prompts and file contents where possible.
Review vendor security and residency terms before deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing and retention controls.
